title: The Window · 5
paragraphs: “And even if it isn’t fine tomorrow,” Mrs. Ramsay said, looking up at William Bankes and Lily Briscoe as they went by, “there’ll be another day. And now—” She was thinking that Lily’s charm lay in her Chinese eyes, set aslant in that small white puckered face, though only a clever man would see it. “And now stand up and let me measure your leg.” They might go to the Lighthouse after all, and she had to check whether the leg of the stocking should be an inch or two longer.

Smiling, because a wonderful idea had flashed on her that very second—William and Lily should marry—she took the heather-mixture stocking, with its crisscross of steel needles at the top, and measured it against James’s leg.

“My dear, stand still,” she said. For James, in his jealousy, did not like serving as a measuring block for the Lighthouse keeper’s little boy, and he fidgeted on purpose; and if he did that, how could she see whether it was too long or too short? she asked.

She glanced up—what demon had got into him, her youngest, her darling?—and her eye fell on the room and on the chairs, and she thought how dreadfully shabby they were. Their guts, as Andrew put it the other day, were spilling all over the floor. But then, she asked herself, why buy good chairs only to have them ruined up here all winter, when the house, with just one old woman to look after it, was absolutely dripping with damp? Never mind. The rent came to exactly twopence halfpenny; the children adored the place; it was good for her husband to be three thousand miles—or, to be accurate, three hundred—away from his library and his lectures and his disciples; and there was space for guests. Mats, camp beds, crazy ghosts of chairs and tables that had finished their years of service in London—up here they did well enough; and so did a photograph or two, and books. Books, she thought, seemed to grow on their own. She never had time to read them. Alas! Even the ones given to her and inscribed by the poet in his own hand—“For her whose wishes must be obeyed” … “The happier Helen of our days” …—it was a disgrace, but she had never read them. And neither Croom on the Mind nor Bates on the Savage Customs of Polynesia (“My dear, stand still,” she said) was something you could send to the Lighthouse. Sooner or later, she supposed, the house would be so shabby that something would have to be done about it. If only they could learn to wipe their feet and stop bringing the beach indoors—that would be something. As for crabs, she had to admit, if Andrew really wanted to dissect them, or if Jasper thought seaweed could be made into soup, there was no stopping it; nor Rose’s collections—shells, reeds, stones; for her children were gifted, though each in a quite different way. And so, she sighed, her eyes taking in the whole room from floor to ceiling while she held the stocking to James’s leg, the result was that things grew shabbier and shabbier, summer after summer. The mat was fading; the wallpaper was coming loose and flapping. Nobody could tell anymore that the pattern was roses. Still, things are bound to spoil if every door in a house stands open all the time and not one locksmith in all Scotland can fix a bolt. What good did it do to drape a green cashmere shawl over the corner of a picture frame? Within two weeks it would be the color of pea soup. But the doors were what annoyed her; every single door was left open. She listened. The drawing-room door stood open; so did the hall door; the bedroom doors sounded open too; and the landing window was certainly open, since she had opened it herself. Windows open, doors shut—simple as that was, could none of them remember it? At night she would go into the maids’ bedrooms and find them shut up tight as ovens—all except Marie’s, the Swiss girl, who would sooner do without a bath than without fresh air. But then at home, the girl had said, “the mountains are so beautiful.” She had said it last night, gazing out of the window with tears in her eyes. “The mountains are so beautiful.” Her father was dying there, as Mrs. Ramsay knew. He was going to leave them fatherless. When the girl spoke, all Mrs. Ramsay’s scolding and demonstrating (how to make a bed, how to open a window, her hands closing and spreading like a Frenchwoman’s) had quietly folded itself around her, just as a bird’s wings fold themselves quietly after a flight through the sunshine, and the blue of its feathers turns from bright steel to soft purple. She had stood there without a word, because there was nothing to say. He had cancer of the throat. Remembering it—how she had stood there, how the girl had said, “At home the mountains are so beautiful,” and how there was no hope, no hope of any kind—she felt a spasm of irritation, and spoke sharply to James:
“Stand still. Don’t be difficult,” so that he knew at once that her sternness was real, and he straightened his leg, and she measured it.
The stocking was too short by at least half an inch, even allowing for the fact that Sorley’s little boy, the Lighthouse keeper’s son, would be smaller than James.
“It’s too short,” she said, “much too short.”

Nobody ever looked so sad. Bitter and black, halfway down, in the dark, in the shaft that ran from the sunlight into the depths, a tear perhaps formed; a tear dropped; the water swayed to and fro, received it, and grew still. Nobody ever looked so sad.

But was it nothing but looks? people said. What was there behind it—her beauty, her splendor? Had he blown his brains out, they asked; had he died the week before they were to be married—some other, earlier lover, rumors of whom reached you? Or was there nothing? Nothing but an incomparable beauty that she lived behind and could do nothing to disturb? For although she could easily have said, at some moment of intimacy, when stories of great passion, of love defeated, of ambition thwarted came her way, that she too had known it, or felt it, or been through it herself, she never spoke. She was always silent. So she knew—she knew without having learned. Her simplicity got to the bottom of what clever people falsified. Her singleness of mind made her drop straight down like a stone, land precisely like a bird; it gave her, naturally, this swoop and fall of the spirit onto the truth, which delighted, eased, sustained—falsely perhaps.

(Once, hearing her voice on the telephone, Mr. Bankes had said, “Nature has but little clay,” deeply moved by it, though all she was telling him was some fact about a train, “like that of which she molded you.” He could see her at the far end of the line: Greek, blue-eyed, with a straight nose. How out of place it felt to be on the telephone to a woman like that. It was as if the Graces had come together and joined hands in fields of asphodel to make that face. Yes, he would take the 10:30 from Euston.

“But she’s no more aware of her beauty than a child is,” said Mr. Bankes, putting down the receiver and crossing the room to see how the workmen were getting on with a hotel they were building at the back of his house. And he thought of Mrs. Ramsay as he watched that bustle among the unfinished walls. For there was always, he thought, something incongruous to be worked into the harmony of her face. She would clap a deerstalker’s hat on her head; she would run across the lawn in galoshes to snatch a child out of mischief. So if it was merely her beauty you thought of, you had to remember the quivering thing, the living thing (they were carrying bricks up a little plank as he watched them), and work it into the picture. Or if you thought of her simply as a woman, you had to give her some freak of idiosyncrasy; or imagine some hidden wish to throw off her royalty of form, as if her beauty bored her, and everything men say about beauty, and she wanted only to be like other people, insignificant. He did not know. He did not know. He must get to his work.)

Mrs. Ramsay went on knitting her hairy, reddish-brown stocking, her head absurdly framed by the gilt picture frame, by the green shawl she had thrown over its edge, and by the authenticated masterpiece by Michelangelo. She smoothed away whatever had been harsh in her manner a moment ago, lifted his head, and kissed her little boy on the forehead. “Let’s find another picture to cut out,” she said.
